Recom- mended duration of treatment varies, but courses are gen- erally of 4 to 8 weeks, depending on response in the first few weeks.2,3,5 However, there is no strong evidence to support this practice,6 and although there are some studies to suggest that antibacterial treatment may be beneficial in inflammatory chronic pelvic pain syndrome, there is less evidence for the non-inflammatory form.3 Other treat- ments that have been tried, with variable results, include2,4-6 the 5α-reductase inhibitor finasteride, alpha blockers such as alfuzosin, terazosin, or tamsulosin, pen- tosan polysulfate sodium, mepartricin, pollen extract, quercetin, and NSAIDs. The role of allopurinol is contro- versial. Non-drug treatments that have shown some prom- ise include transurethral or transrectal microwave thermotherapy2,4-6 and sacral nerve stimulation.5 Stress management therapy has also been tried.2 Drugs used for symptomatic relief of neuropathic pain may include tricy- clic antidepressants such as amitriptyline, or antiepileptics such as gabapentin. Anticholinergics such as oxybutynin or tolterodine may be used for urinary frequency.5 Asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis (category IV) is often detected coincidentally during examination for other disorders.1 1. Renal calculi The solubility of calcium, oxalate, and phosphate in nor- mal urine is maintained by a variety of inhibitors of crys- tallisation, both organic and inorganic. However, increases in the concentrations of crystalline substances in the urine, or decreases in the relative proportions of crystallisation inhibitors, may render individuals susceptible to urolithia- sis, the formation of renal calculi (kidney stones).
